messages.author: 6e0bce06355e4e6c
messages.subject: Change of variables
parts:
Dear STAN users

I have a mathematical question (so perhaps not suited for the list) but I'm sufficiently stuck to give it a try. I want to assign (~) a matrix_normal_prec() to a logit-transformed matrix, of which the individual elements are the sum of several elements from a Dirichlet() distribution. I've attached the model and dataset and have used a development version from Marcus to be able to access the matrix_normal distribution. The question is how to correct lp__ for the logit transformation / change of variables? I understand a simple example (e.g. the logit transformation of a scalar, similar to several examples in the manual), but here I have a full matrix and a summation, and I'm not sure how the correction works in such a case. Perhaps someone with better math-skills than me can help out (!), thanks in advance.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Change of variables
parts:
If y are the unconstrained values and x = f(y) are
the constrained values, then if you write

x ~ foo(theta);

you need to add the log of the absolute determinant of
the Jacobian matrix for the transform f. The entries
J[m,n] in the Jacobian are:

J[m,n] = d/d.y[m] { f(y)[n] }

I don't understand the intent of what you're doing, but you
have two priors on the matrix, one from the sampling statement on
logit_r1 and one from the sampling statement on phi.

If you just put the priors on phi, you can transform and use
the result as a parameter w/o a Jacobian adjustment. If you drop
the priors on phi and go with a prior on logit_r1, then you'll need
the Jacobian of the transform. If you leave them both, it's essentially
a product prior.

a ~ foo(theta);
a ~ bar(rho);

means

p(a) propto foo(a|theta) * bar(a|rho);

It doesn't look like the derivatives are too bad, but
all the indexing looks like it's going to be fiddly unless
you can reexpress in terms of simpler vectors.

- Bob

Dear Bob,

I just had an appointment with someone from our Biostatistics department to help me with the change in variables. However, we still got stuck and were hoping that you could explain your suggestion for a very simple example (attached below)?

Thank you very much,
Marcel


parameters{
  simplex[4] phi[2];
}

transformed parameters{
 vector[2] logit_r1;
 logit_r1[1] <- logit( phi[1,3] + phi[1,4] );
 logit_r1[2] <- logit( phi[2,3] + phi[2,4] );
}

model{
 phi[1] ~ dirichlet( [....] );
 phi[2] ~ dirichlet( [....] );
 logit_r1 ~ multi_normal_prec( [..] , [..,..] );
 // account for change in variables
 lp__ <- lp__ + ..
}

> Dear Bob,

> I just had an appointment with someone from our Biostatistics department to help me with the change in variables.
> However, we still got stuck and were hoping that you could explain your suggestion for a very simple example (attached

> phi[2] ~ dirichlet( [....] );
> logit_r1 ~ multi_normal_prec( [..] , [..,..] );
> // account for change in variables
> lp__ <- lp__ + ..
> }

Why do you want to parameterize like this? It seems
like it's asking for non-identifiability. Or is there
something else going on with the phi?

The way you have it parameterized, you actually put
priors on phi twice, once through phi itself and once
in the transformed form with logit_r1 ~. Is that
really what you intended? It might be if the arguments
to multi_norm_prec are reversed, because

y ~ multi_normal_prec(mu,Omega)

does the same thing as

mu ~ multi_normal_prec(y,Omega);

So what's the first arg to multi_normal_prec?

I'm really bad at this myself. Ben's always helped me out.
Hopefully he'll chime in here.

Technically, you need to calculate the determinant of
the Jacobian of the multivariate transform. Where I always
get stuck is figuring out what the transform dimensions are.
And it tends to work out that the determinant is easy because
the the Jacobian is diagonal or lower triangular.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Change of variables
parts:
On Friday, September 13, 2013 1:53:52 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I'm really bad at this myself.  Ben's always helped me out.
Hopefully he'll chime in here.

I agree that in the stated example it is not exactly clear if this is sensible. But just so that anyone who might google this thread is clear, we are talking about

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_density_function#Dependent_variables_and_change_of_variables

which is sort of a fundamental principle of statistics but one that comes up a lot more with Stan than with, say, maximum likelihood.

Ben

messages.author: 6e0bce06355e4e6c
messages.subject: RE: [stan-users] Change of variables
parts:
Dear Ben, Bob,

There's no typo. The data are very sparse and the additional (improper) prior on the sum of several elements of phi is intended to allow for a spatial pooling of strength via a MVCAR distribution. We thought about other specifications too, but theoretically it makes sense to smooth via the sums of several elements of phi instead of individual elements of phi. Perhaps phi also converges without the dirichlet (in the actual model there are several combinations of elements of phi that each get their own MVCAR) but also here the transformations need to be accounted for. Ben, is this transformation mathematically possible?

Thank you..(!)
